crqs.questionText:
Differentiate command line interface (CLI) and graphical user interface (GUI) on the basis of the given aspects.

| Aspect | CLI | GUI |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Style of Interaction | | |
| Use of Resource | | |
| Feedback on Error | | |
| Accessibility | | |
crqs.currentSloDescription: explain the following types of system software: a. operating system, b. device drivers, c. utility programs, d. language processors;

rubric.description: 1 mark for correct differentiation on Style of Interaction (typing text commands vs clicking icons/menus).
1 mark for correct differentiation on Use of Resource (low memory/keyboard-only vs higher RAM/CPU and mouse/I-O devices).
1 mark for correct differentiation on Feedback on Error (text command error lines vs visual pop-up dialogs/alerts).
1 mark for correct differentiation on Accessibility (less accessible/requires memorising commands vs highly accessible/intuitive visual icons).

crqs.modelAnswer:
| Aspect | Command Line Interface (CLI) | Graphical User Interface (GUI) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Style of Interaction** | User interacts by typing text-based commands via the keyboard at a command prompt. | User interacts visually by clicking icons, menus, windows, and buttons using a mouse or touchscreen. |
| **Use of Resource** | Consumes very little system memory (RAM) and CPU processing power; requires only a keyboard and basic display. | Consumes significantly more system memory (RAM), GPU/CPU resources, and uses pointing devices (mouse/touchscreen). |
| **Feedback on Error** | Displays text-based syntax or command error messages directly in the terminal lines. | Displays visual pop-up dialog boxes, alert icons, or sound prompts when an error occurs. |
| **Accessibility** | Less accessible for beginners because users must memorise exact command syntax and parameters. | Highly accessible and user-friendly for beginners because visual icons and menus are intuitive. |
crqs.betterResponse: In better responses, candidates showed a clear understanding of the concept and wrote accurate points for each aspect: CLI by typing commands vs GUI by clicking on the interface; fewer vs more hardware/memory resources; error feedback through command text vs visual pop-ups; and CLI being less accessible for novices while GUI is more accessible.
crqs.weakerResponse: In weaker responses, candidates mixed up CLI and GUI in the style of interaction, gave vague terms in the use of resources (e.g., 'they use RAM and ROM'), and wrote unclear points on feedback and accessibility without highlighting key differences.
crqs.suggestions: Review the 2025 E-Marking Notes for examiner commentary on better vs weaker responses.

crqs.questionText: Write any TWO features of analog signals.

rubric.description: 1 mark for stating first valid feature of analog signals (e.g., continuous wave form that varies smoothly over time).
1 mark for stating second valid feature (e.g., represents physical quantities such as temperature, sound, or pressure with continuous amplitude/frequency).

crqs.modelAnswer:
**Features of Analog Signals (Any TWO — 2 Marks):**
1. **Continuous Wave Form:** An analog signal is a continuous wave (sine wave) that changes smoothly over time and can take an infinite number of values within a given range.
2. **Represents Physical Quantities:** It directly represents natural physical quantities such as sound waves, temperature, light intensity, and atmospheric pressure, characterised by continuous amplitude and frequency.

crqs.questionText: Compare Wide Area Network (WAN) with Local Area Network (LAN) by giving any TWO disadvantages of WAN.
crqs.currentSloDescription: explain different types of computer networks, i.e., Local Area Network (LAN), Wide Area Network (WAN), and Metropolitan Area Network (MAN), highlighting their characteristics and applications;

rubric.description: 1 mark for first valid disadvantage of WAN compared to LAN (e.g., expensive setup/maintenance cost).
1 mark for second valid disadvantage of WAN compared to LAN (e.g., higher latency, lower speed/bandwidth, complex security/maintenance, or dependence on service providers).

crqs.modelAnswer:
**Disadvantages of WAN Compared to LAN (Any TWO — 2 Marks):**
1. **Higher Setup & Maintenance Cost:** A WAN is significantly more expensive to set up and maintain than a LAN because it spans cities/countries and requires leased telecommunication lines, routers, or satellite links.
2. **Higher Latency & Lower Data Transfer Speed:** Due to vast geographical distances and multiple intermediate hops, WANs experience higher propagation delay (latency), lower effective bandwidth, and greater security/administration complexity than a local LAN.
crqs.betterResponse: In better responses, candidates clearly stated precise disadvantages of WAN compared to LAN: WAN is expensive to set up and maintain, has higher latency, lower bandwidth, and depends on external ISP/telecom service providers.
crqs.weakerResponse: In weaker responses, candidates mixed up advantages of WAN (covering a large geographical area) with disadvantages, or wrote vague statements like 'WAN signals are disturbed by other radio waves'.

erqs.questionText:
**EITHER**
**a.**
i. Draw the block diagram of a computer system. (2 Marks)
ii. Describe the function of any FOUR components of block diagram drawn in part i. (4 Marks)

erqs.originalSloText: illustrate the Von Neumann Architecture using a block diagram;
erqs.currentSloDescription: illustrate the Von Neumann Architecture using a block diagram;

rubric.description: Part a(i): Draws a labelled block diagram showing Input, CPU (CU & ALU), Memory, and Output units (2 Marks); OR Part b: Healthcare big data application with example (2 Marks).
Part a(ii): Accurately describes the function of first two components (2 Marks); OR Part b: IoT big data application with example (2 Marks).
Part a(ii): Accurately describes the function of remaining two components (2 Marks); OR Part b: Manufacturing big data application with example (2 Marks).

erqs.modelAnswer:
**Option a (Von Neumann / Computer System Block Diagram):**
- **i. Block Diagram (2 Marks):** `Input Unit` $\rightarrow$ `Central Processing Unit (Control Unit + Arithmetic Logic Unit)` $\leftrightarrow$ `Memory Unit (Primary & Secondary Storage)` $\rightarrow$ `Output Unit`.
- **ii. Functions of Four Components (4 Marks):**
  1. **Input Unit:** Accepts raw data and instructions from the user via devices like keyboard, mouse, or sensors and converts them into binary form.
  2. **Control Unit (CU):** Directs and coordinates all operations inside the computer by fetching, decoding, and managing instruction execution signals.
  3. **Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU):** Performs all arithmetic calculations ($+, -, \times, \div$) and logical comparisons ($<, >, =$).
  4. **Memory Unit / Output Unit:** Memory stores data and instructions temporarily (RAM) or permanently (SSD/HDD), while the Output Unit converts processed binary results into human-readable form on screens or printers.

**Option b (Purpose of Big Data in Three Fields — 6 Marks):**
1. **Healthcare (2 Marks):** Analyses electronic health records (EHRs), wearable patient monitors, and genomic datasets to predict disease outbreaks, personalise treatment plans, and detect early clinical warning signs.
2. **Internet of Things (IoT) (2 Marks):** Processes continuous real-time sensor streams from smart homes, connected vehicles, and smart city grids to automate energy conservation and traffic control.
3. **Manufacturing (2 Marks):** Uses industrial sensor telemetry for predictive maintenance of factory machinery, automated defect detection on assembly lines, and supply-chain inventory optimisation.

erqs.questionText:
**EITHER**
**a.**
i. Compare primary and secondary storage devices based on their location with respect to the Central Processing Unit (CPU). (2 Marks)
ii. Discuss the function of primary and secondary storage devices for data processing in real-time scenarios. (4 Marks)

**OR**
**b.**
i. Explain the differences between impact and non-impact printers with TWO examples. (3 Marks)
ii. Give ONE advantage of using laser printers in a modern office environment focusing on speed, print quality and operational costs each. (3 Marks)
erqs.currentSloDescription: describe primary and secondary storage devices based on location, cost, capacity, access time, data processing method, and storage technology such as semiconductor (SSD), magnetic (HDD), and optical;

rubric.description: Part a(i): 1 mark each for comparing location of primary (on motherboard near CPU) and secondary storage (farther/external via I/O) (2 Marks); OR Part b(i): 1 mark for difference between impact and non-impact printers + 2 marks for examples (3 Marks).

Part a(ii): 1 mark for each highlighted point on real-time processing in primary vs permanent retention in secondary storage (4 Marks); OR Part b(ii): 1 mark each for advantage of laser printers in speed, print quality, and operational costs (3 Marks).

erqs.modelAnswer:
**Option a (Primary vs. Secondary Storage Devices — 6 Marks):**
- **i. Location with Respect to CPU (2 Marks):**
  - **Primary Storage (RAM/ROM):** Located directly on the motherboard very close to the CPU and communicates directly with the processor via the high-speed system bus.
  - **Secondary Storage (HDD/SSD/Optical/USB):** Located farther away from the CPU (connected via I/O controllers or external ports) and cannot be accessed directly by the CPU without first loading data into RAM.
- **ii. Function in Real-Time Data Processing Scenarios (4 Marks):**
  1. **Primary Storage Function (2 Marks):** Holds currently executing programs and live incoming data streams (e.g., active calculations or real-time sensor readings) for ultra-fast, nanosecond retrieval and manipulation by the CPU.
  2. **Secondary Storage Function (2 Marks):** Provides high-capacity, non-volatile permanent storage for archiving completed files, databases, and operating system installations (e.g., saving an Excel spreadsheet onto an SSD or USB drive) after real-time processing is complete.

**Option b (Impact vs. Non-Impact Printers & Laser Printer Advantages — 6 Marks):**
- **i. Differences & Two Examples (3 Marks):**
  - **Difference (1 Mark):** **Impact printers** form characters by physically striking an inked ribbon against the paper using pins or hammers (producing loud noise and lower speed), whereas **non-impact printers** form characters and images without physical contact with the paper using laser beams, toner, or ink spray (operating quietly at high speed).
  - **Two Examples (2 Marks):**
    - *Impact Printer Examples:* Dot-Matrix Printer, Daisy-Wheel Printer (or Line Printer).
    - *Non-Impact Printer Examples:* Laser Printer, Inkjet Printer (or Thermal Printer).
- **ii. Advantages of Laser Printers in a Modern Office (3 Marks):**
  1. **Speed (1 Mark):** Prints entire pages at once (page printer) at high speeds (20–60+ pages per minute), handling large office workloads rapidly.
  2. **Print Quality (1 Mark):** Produces razor-sharp, high-resolution text and graphics (600–2400 DPI) free from ink smudging.
  3. **Operational Costs (1 Mark):** Has a very low cost per page in high-volume office printing because a single toner cartridge prints thousands of pages.
erqs.betterResponse: In 5a, better responses clearly contrasted primary memory (near/directly connected to CPU for immediate fast processing) with secondary storage (farther/external for permanent storage). In 5b, better responses contrasted electromechanical ribbon striking in impact printers (Dot Matrix) with non-contact laser/inkjet printing and gave specific points on speed, DPI quality, and low per-page toner cost.
erqs.weakerResponse: In 5a, weaker responses confused SSD/HDD as primary storage or claimed primary memory stores data permanently. In 5b, weaker responses claimed impact printers are 'more advanced and portable' or gave vague statements about laser printers without addressing speed, print quality, and operational cost.
erqs.suggestions: Review the 2025 E-Marking Notes for examiner commentary on better vs weaker responses.

erqs.questionText:
**EITHER**
**a.**
i. Write TWO differences between guided (wired) and unguided (wireless) media. (2 Marks)
ii. Describe any TWO examples of guided media. (4 Marks)

**OR**
**b.**
i. Define network topology. (1 Mark)
ii. Give any FOUR benefits of using ring topology as compared to other topologies (bus, star, mesh). (4 Marks)
iii. Draw the diagram of ring topology. (1 Mark)
erqs.currentSloDescription: explain guided media and unguided media;

rubric.description: Part a(i): 1 mark for each complete difference between guided and unguided media (2 Marks); OR Part b(i)+(iii): 1 mark for defining network topology + 1 mark for ring topology diagram (2 Marks).
Part a(ii): 2 marks for each guided media example (2 statements per example = 4 Marks); OR Part b(ii): 1 mark for each of four valid benefits of ring topology (4 Marks).

erqs.modelAnswer:
**Option a (Guided vs. Unguided Media — 6 Marks):**
- **i. Two Differences between Guided and Unguided Media (2 Marks):**
  1. **Physical Pathway:** In **guided (wired) media**, data signals travel along a solid physical conductor (copper wire or glass optical fibre), whereas in **unguided (wireless) media**, electromagnetic signals propagate freely through air or vacuum without physical cables.
  2. **Directionality & Security:** Guided media provides a directed point-to-point path with higher security and less interference, whereas unguided media broadcasts signals omnidirectionally or line-of-sight and is more susceptible to atmospheric interference and eavesdropping.
- **ii. Two Examples of Guided Media (4 Marks — 2 Marks each):**
  1. **Twisted-Pair Cable (2 Marks):** Consists of pairs of insulated copper wires twisted together to reduce electromagnetic interference (EMI); widely used in Ethernet LANs in two forms: Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) and Shielded Twisted Pair (STP).
  2. **Fibre-Optic Cable (or Coaxial Cable) (2 Marks):** Consists of a thin glass or plastic core surrounded by cladding that transmits data as pulses of light using total internal reflection, offering extremely high bandwidth and immunity to electromagnetic noise.

**Option b (Network Topology & Ring Topology — 6 Marks):**
- **i. Definition of Network Topology (1 Mark):** Network topology is the physical or logical layout/arrangement of computers, cables, and networking devices in a communication network.
- **ii. Four Benefits of Ring Topology Compared to Bus/Star/Mesh (4 Marks):**
  1. **No Central Server/Hub Required:** Unlike star topology, it does not require a central hub or switch to manage connectivity between nodes.
  2. **Organised Unidirectional Data Flow (No Collisions):** Data packets travel in one direction around the ring using token passing, eliminating packet collisions common in bus topology.
  3. **Lower Cabling Cost than Mesh/Star:** Requires significantly less cabling than mesh or star topology since each node only connects to its two immediate neighbours.
  4. **Equal Access for All Nodes:** Every workstation has equal opportunity to transmit data via the token, preventing a single node from monopolising bandwidth.
- **iii. Diagram of Ring Topology (1 Mark):**
  - A closed circular loop connecting `Node 1` $\rightarrow$ `Node 2` $\rightarrow$ `Node 3` $\rightarrow$ `Node 4` $\rightarrow$ back to `Node 1`.
erqs.betterResponse: In 6a, better responses contrasted physical wire pathways vs air/wireless propagation and described twisted-pair, coaxial, and fibre-optic cables with two clear statements each. In 6b, better responses defined network topology accurately, listed four distinct advantages of ring topology, and drew a closed loop connecting all computer nodes.
erqs.weakerResponse: In 6a, weaker responses gave vague statements and listed 'cameras, printers, and TV' as examples of guided media instead of twisted-pair, coaxial, or fibre-optic cables. In 6b, weaker responses confused ring topology with bus or star topology.

crqs.originalSloText: solve the trace table for a given flowchart.

rubric.description: Correctly determines the value of X for Iteration 1 (X = 3, or initial X = 1).
Correctly determines the value of X for Iteration 2 (X = 5, or 3).
Correctly determines the value of X for Iteration 3 (X = 7, or 5) where X > 5 terminates the loop.

crqs.modelAnswer:
**Trace Table Solution:**
- Initial state before loop: `Set X = 1`
- **Iteration 1:** Condition `IF X > 5` (`1 > 5` is NO) $\rightarrow$ `X = X + 2 = 1 + 2 = 3` (or if tracking X entering each check: Iteration 1 = `3`, Iteration 2 = `5`, Iteration 3 = `7`, after which `7 > 5` is YES and the flowchart stops).

| Iterations | Value of X (after `X = X + 2`) |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 3 |
| 2 | 5 |
| 3 | 7 |

crqs.modelAnswer:
### i. Boolean Expression & Logic Circuit Architecture (3 Marks)
- **Condition 1:** `Switch A = 1 OR Switch B = 0` $\rightarrow (A + \overline{B})$
- **Condition 2:** `Switch A = 0 OR Switch B = 0` $\rightarrow (\overline{A} + \overline{B})$
- **Condition 3:** `Switch A = 1 OR Switch B = 1` $\rightarrow (A + B)$

Determine whether the following expressions of GW-BASIC will be evaluated as TRUE (`1`) or FALSE (`0`).

| GW-BASIC Expression | True/ False |
| :--- | :---: |
| `PRINT (3 * 3 / 3) > 3` | |
| `PRINT (20 MOD 7) < 8` | |
| `PRINT (5 + 5 - 5 * 5 / 5) = 5` | |

crqs.markingHints:

crqs.modelAnswer:
### Part (a): Power Calculation ($P = I \times V$)
**GW-BASIC Program (2019 Exam):**
```basic
10 CLS
20 INPUT "Current: "; I
30 INPUT "Voltage: "; V
40 LET P = I * V
50 PRINT "Power = "; P
60 END
```

**2025 Syllabus Equivalent (JavaScript):**
```javascript
let I = parseFloat(prompt("Enter current (I):"));
let V = parseFloat(prompt("Enter voltage (V):"));
let P = I * V;
document.write("Power (P) = " + P);
```

### Part (b): Evaluating Operator Expressions
| GW-BASIC Expression | Step-by-Step Evaluation | True / False |
| :--- | :--- | :---: |
| `PRINT (3 * 3 / 3) > 3` | `(9 / 3) > 3` $\Rightarrow 3 > 3$ | **False (`0`)** |
| `PRINT (20 MOD 7) < 8` | `6 < 8` (since $20 = 2 \times 7 + 6$) | **True (`1`)** |
| `PRINT (5 + 5 - 5 * 5 / 5) = 5` | `(5 + 5 - 25 / 5) = (10 - 5) = 5` | **True (`1`)** |
| `PRINT (1 AND 0 OR 1 AND 0) = 1` | `(0 OR 0) = 1` $\Rightarrow 0 = 1$ | **False (`0`)** |

Part (a): Questions related to arithmetic operations in GW-BASIC were well attempted.

Part (b): Questions related to arithmetic, relational, and logical operators were generally well attempted.
crqs.betterResponse:
Part (a): Better responses demonstrated strong understanding of basic concepts of GW-BASIC programming. These responses wrote correct input and output statements and used * operator for multiplication in GW-BASIC statement to calculate power rather than using × as multiplication operator.

Part (b): Better responses depicted strong understanding of almost all types of GW-BASIC operators and their evaluation in GW-BASIC statements, i.e. arithmetic operators, relational operators and logic operators.
crqs.weakerResponse:
Part (a): Weaker responses showed poor understanding of the basic concepts of GW-BASIC programming. These responses used mathematical multiplication operator rather than multiplication operator (*) of programming / these responses used values for voltage and current to calculate power just like a numerical rather than writing programming code for it. Most of these responses managed to correctly write the code to either print output or take input but struggled to write the formula of power in the form of GW-BASIC instruction. Likewise, another common mistake made by some of these responses was not using the comma between the message and variable name in the input statement and in output statement inverted commas were used around the name of the variable rather than writing it without commas.

Part (b): Weaker responses were mostly unable to evaluate the second and the fourth GW-BASIC statements. It shows that candidates had poor understanding of modulus (MOD) and logic operators. However, most of these responses managed to evaluate the first and third GW-BASIC statements correctly that contain the arithmetic and relational operators.
crqs.suggestions: Ensure students use the programming multiplication operator `*` instead of the algebraic `×` symbol and distinguish between string literals in quotes and variable names. Practice evaluating compound expressions combining modulus (`MOD` / `%`), arithmetic, relational, and logical (`AND`/`&&`, `OR`/`||`) operators step by step.

erqs.modelAnswer:
### Option (a): USB Virus Threats & Prevention Steps

### i. Six Possible Threats to the PC from a Virus-Infected USB Drive:
1. **Corruption or Deletion of Data & Files:** The virus can overwrite, corrupt, or permanently delete documents, media, and program files.
2. **Boot Sector Damage:** Boot-sector viruses can overwrite the Master Boot Record (MBR), preventing the operating system from booting.
3. **File Replication & Shortcut Creation:** Viruses/worms can hide original folders, replace them with malicious `.exe`/`.lnk` shortcuts, and self-replicate until disk space is exhausted.
4. **System Slowdown & Resource Exhaustion:** Malicious background processes consume CPU cycles and RAM, causing severe system lag and frequent crashes.
5. **Theft of Confidential Information:** Spyware or Trojans carried on the USB drive can steal saved passwords, financial records, and personal files.
6. **Propagation Across Connected Networks:** Once inside the PC, the malware can spread to shared drives and other computers on the local network.

### ii. Preventive Steps to Avoid Virus Infection:
1. **Install & Update Antivirus Software:** Keep real-time antivirus protection and virus definitions up to date.
2. **Scan External Drives Before Opening:** Always scan any newly connected USB flash drive with antivirus software before accessing its files.
3. **Disable AutoRun / Avoid Double-Clicking:** Disable USB AutoRun and open drives via the folder tree rather than double-clicking the root icon.
4. **Maintain Regular Backups & OS Updates:** Keep offline/cloud backups of critical files and install operating system security patches promptly.

### Option (b): Artificial Intelligence in Defence & Weather Forecasting

### 1. Uses of Artificial Intelligence in the Defence Industry:
- **Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs / Drones) & Autonomous Robots:** AI powers reconnaissance drones, bomb-disposal robots, and autonomous ground vehicles to patrol borders and neutralise threats.
- **Target Recognition & Threat Surveillance:** Computer vision and sensor-fusion algorithms analyse radar and satellite imagery in real time to detect enemy movement and guide precision defense systems.
- **Combat Simulation & Cybersecurity:** AI models simulate battlefield scenarios for military training and defend critical military networks against cyberattacks.

### 2. Uses of Artificial Intelligence in Weather Forecasting:
- **Satellite & Radar Pattern Analysis:** Machine-learning models process massive meteorological datasets (atmospheric pressure, wind speed, humidity, ocean temperatures) from satellites and weather stations.
- **Severe Storm & Natural Disaster Prediction:** AI predicts cyclones, flash floods, heatwaves, and heavy rainfall patterns days in advance.

### 3. Key Benefits of Using AI in Defence & Weather Forecasting:
1. **Protection of Human Life:** Autonomous defense robots and drones can operate 24/7 in hazardous combat zones or minefields without risking soldiers' lives.
2. **High Precision & Early Disaster Warnings:** AI analyses millions of meteorological variables far faster and more accurately than manual methods, providing early evacuation alerts that save lives and reduce property damage.

1. **Worm (2 Marks):** A standalone malicious program that **self-replicates** and spreads automatically across computer networks and the internet without requiring a host program or human intervention, consuming network bandwidth and system memory.
2. **Adware (2 Marks):** Advertising-supported software that automatically displays or downloads unwanted pop-up advertisements and banners onto a user's screen or browser, often bundled with free software and tracking user browsing habits.
3. **Trojan Horse (2 Marks):** Malicious software disguised as a legitimate, useful, or desirable application to trick users into installing and executing it. Unlike viruses or worms, a Trojan horse does not self-replicate, but opens backdoors, steals credentials, or grants remote control to attackers.

### Option (b): Types of Hackers
1. **Script Kiddie (2 Marks):** An unskilled individual who lacks deep programming or networking expertise and uses pre-written scripts, automated tools, or exploit kits created by other hackers to launch cyberattacks for thrill or notoriety.
2. **Blue Hat Hacker (2 Marks):** Outside security testers invited by software companies (such as Microsoft) to test a system for bugs and vulnerabilities prior to its public launch (or amateur hackers motivated by personal revenge).
3. **Red Hat Hacker (2 Marks):** Vigilante hackers who combine ethical intent with aggressive tactics; instead of merely reporting black hat hackers to authorities, they infiltrate black hat infrastructure and launch counter-attacks to destroy malicious servers and botnets.
erqs.examinerComments:
Part (a): Though part a of the question was not opted for by the majority, from the ones who attempted it, only some of the candidates demonstrated a clear understanding of the topic. They explained the required terms accurately using the correct definitions supported with suitable examples, whereas others confused the characteristics of malware, missed key points like the self-replication of worms, and gave vague or incorrect statements about adware and Trojans.

Part (b): Majority of the students attempted this question. Yet, the overall performance was not satisfactory. Some candidates succeeded by giving accurate definitions with examples, such as describing script kiddies as lacking technical skills and Blue Hat Hackers as experimenters. However, many showed confusion by mixing up hacker types, especially Blue Hat with Green Hat, and failed to clearly separate ethical from unethical hackers.
erqs.betterResponse:
Part (a): In better responses, candidates provided clear and well-structured explanations of the terms worm, adware, and Trojan horse. For example, a worm transmits itself over a network to infect other computers. Adware displays advertisements to users. Trojans are disguised as legitimate or desirable software to trick users into executing them. They accurately identified the key characteristics of each type of malware, elaborating on how they spread within systems and networks.

Part (b): In better responses, candidates effectively defined the distinct characteristics of the three types of hackers. For example, a script kiddie lacks technical expertise or skills but uses pre-made scripts to conduct cyberattacks. Blue hat hacker is neither a white hat nor a black hat, either invited by organisations to test systems for bugs before launch or seeking revenge, while Red Hat hackers act as vigilantes who aggressively target and disable black hat hackers.
erqs.weakerResponse:
Part (a): In weaker responses, candidates confused the characteristics of different types of malware and were unable to clearly state the key definitions. For example, in the case of worms, they frequently missed essential points such as the worm's ability to self-replicate and spread automatically across computer networks without user intervention.

Part (b): In weaker responses, candidates did not perform well on this question and struggled to differentiate between the various types of hackers, particularly Blue Hat Hackers. Some confused them with Green Hat Hackers, while others mixed up the definitions of Red Hat Hackers and Black Hat Hackers. Additionally, several responses failed to distinguish between ethical and unethical hackers.
erqs.suggestions:
Teachers are encouraged to facilitate classroom discussions or debates focused on the definitions, characteristics, and differences between various types of malware.
Engaging students in comparative discussions will help reinforce their understanding and clarify misconceptions, ensuring they can clearly distinguish between threats like worms, adware, and Trojan horses.
Teachers can incorporate interactive activities such as role plays, PowerPoint presentations, or group-based class presentations to enhance students' understanding of different types of hackers.
By assigning each group a specific type of hacker to research and present, students can engage more deeply with the content in a memorable way.

erqs.modelAnswer:
### i. Authentication vs. Authorisation (2 Marks)
- **Authentication (1 Mark):** The process of verifying the **identity** of a user, device, or system before granting access (e.g., verifying a username and password, PIN, access card, or biometric scan).
- **Authorisation (1 Mark):** The process of determining what **permissions, privileges, or resources** an already-authenticated user is allowed to access or perform (e.g., read-only vs. administrator access).

### ii. Two Methods for Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) (4 Marks)
1. **Password/PIN + One-Time Password (SMS / Authenticator App OTP) (2 Marks):** Combines *something the user knows* (account password) with *something the user has* (a time-sensitive verification code sent to their registered mobile phone or generated by an authenticator app).
2. **Access Card + Biometric Scan / PIN (2 Marks):** Combines *something the user has* (a physical smart card / ATM card) with *something the user is* (fingerprint or facial recognition scan) or *knows* (confidential PIN) to grant secure access to banking or restricted facilities.

### Types of Hackers (6 Marks)
1. **White Hat Hacker (2 Marks):** Also known as **ethical hackers**, these cybersecurity professionals are **authorised** by organisations to perform penetration testing, identify security vulnerabilities, and fix system weaknesses before malicious attackers can exploit them.
2. **Black Hat Hacker (2 Marks):** Malicious cybercriminals who break into computer systems and networks **without authorisation** to steal sensitive data, extort money (ransomware), distribute malware, or damage systems for personal or financial gain.
3. **Green Hat Hacker (2 Marks):** Amateur or novice hackers ('newbies') who are new to the hacking world, lack advanced technical expertise, and are eager to learn hacking techniques and tools from experienced hackers in online communities.
erqs.examinerComments:
Part (a): As this was an ERQ question, majority of the candidates attempted this part. The overall responses in this question were commendable, as the candidates demonstrated a good understanding of authorisation and authentication methods by relating them to general life practices.

Part (b): As this was the ERQ, few candidates attempted this part. The overall performance of the candidates in this question was impressive, as it pertained to a commonly discussed and observed topic in daily life.

Part (b): In better responses, candidates showed commendable understanding of the three types of hackers, providing accurate definitions and clear distinctions between each category: white hat hackers as ethical hackers, black hat hackers as criminals, and green hat hackers as learners of cybersecurity.

Part (b): Weaker responses provided vague or inaccurate statements, such as calling white hat hackers 'the best hackers', black hat hackers 'the most dangerous hackers', and green hat hackers 'not too dangerous hackers' without defining their intent, authorization, or skill level.

### Option (a): Impacts of Computers on Society

### Four Positive Impacts of Computers on Society:
1. **Fast Global Communication:** Enables instant long-distance communication, email, and video conferencing, saving time and travel costs.
2. **Remote Work & Employment Opportunities:** Creates new jobs in IT, software development, e-commerce, and online freelancing, allowing individuals to work from home globally.
3. **Accessible E-Learning & Education:** Provides access to online courses, digital libraries, and virtual classrooms from world-class institutions.
4. **Paperless Environment & Fast Public Services:** Automates banking, healthcare, and airline reservation systems while reducing paper consumption and environmental waste.

### Four Negative Impacts of Computers on Society:
1. **Health & Well-Being Risks:** Prolonged screen time and poor posture cause eye strain, headaches, musculoskeletal pain, and obesity from physical inactivity.
2. **Social Isolation:** Excessive use of digital devices and social media reduces face-to-face family and community interaction.
3. **Rapid Spread of Misinformation & Cyberbullying:** Online platforms can be misused to spread rumours, fake news, and cyberbullying.
4. **Automation & Job Displacement:** Computerised automation of manual clerical and factory tasks can displace unskilled workers.

### Option (b): Importance of Software Licensing (User's vs. Owner's View)

### Importance of Software Licensing — User's Point of View (4 Points):
1. **Protection from Malware & Viruses:** Licensed software comes from verified publishers and is free from hidden Trojans, spyware, or ransomware often bundled in pirated copies.
2. **Official Updates & Security Patches:** Licensed users receive regular bug fixes, feature upgrades, and security patches.
3. **Technical Support & Documentation:** Users gain access to official customer support, manuals, and warranty assistance.
4. **Legal & Ethical Compliance:** Using licensed software protects individuals and organisations from copyright infringement penalties and legal prosecution.

### Importance of Software Licensing — Owner's / Developer's Point of View (4 Points):
1. **Fair Financial Compensation:** Licensing ensures developers and software companies are paid for their time, effort, and investment.
2. **Intellectual Property & Copyright Protection:** Prevents unauthorised copying, redistribution, or reverse-engineering of proprietary code.
3. **Funding Research & Future Versions:** Revenue from software licences funds ongoing R&D, maintenance, and development of improved future releases.
4. **Control Over Usage Terms:** Allows the owner to define clear legal terms regarding the number of installations, commercial use, and liability.

### Option (a): Computer Viruses — Definition, Spread & Prevention

### i. Definition of a Computer Virus (1 Mark):
A **computer virus** is a malicious software program capable of replicating itself by attaching its code to legitimate files or the boot sector, damaging data, corrupting files, and disrupting normal computer operations without the user's permission.

### ii. Three Ways Computer Viruses Spread (3 Marks):
1. **Infected Removable Storage Media:** Connecting infected USB flash drives, external hard disks, or optical discs and opening files on them.
2. **Phishing & Infected Email Attachments:** Opening malicious attachments or links received in emails from unknown or spoofed senders.
3. **Pirated Software & Untrusted Internet Downloads:** Downloading cracked software, pirated games, or infected files from insecure websites or peer-to-peer networks.

### iii. Four Steps to Protect a Computer System Against Viruses (4 Marks):
1. **Install & Update Antivirus Software:** Run reputable antivirus software with real-time protection and updated virus definitions.
2. **Scan External Drives Before Use:** Always scan USB flash drives and external media before opening any files.
3. **Enable a Firewall & Keep the OS Patched:** Keep the operating system and firewall updated to block network-borne exploits.
4. **Avoid Untrusted Email Attachments & Pirated Software:** Never open suspicious email attachments or install unlicensed/pirated programs.

### Option (b): Hacking — Definition & Seven Preventive Measures

### Definition of Hacking (1 Mark):
**Hacking** is the act of gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, network, or digital account to view, steal, modify, or destroy sensitive data or disrupt system operations.

### Seven Effective Measures to Prevent Hacking (7 Marks):
1. **Use Strong, Unique Passwords & Change Them Periodically:** Combine uppercase/lowercase letters, digits, and symbols, and avoid reusing passwords across accounts.
2. **Enable Two-Factor Authentication (2FA):** Require a secondary verification code in addition to a password when signing in.
3. **Enable Hardware/Software Firewalls:** Monitor and filter incoming and outgoing network traffic to block unauthorized intrusion attempts.
4. **Keep the Operating System & Applications Updated:** Install security patches promptly to close software vulnerabilities.
5. **Install Antivirus & Anti-Spyware Software:** Detect and remove keyloggers, Trojans, and remote-access malware.
6. **Avoid Logging into Sensitive Accounts on Public Computers/Wi-Fi:** Never access banking or personal accounts on untrusted public terminals or unsecured Wi-Fi networks.
7. **Beware of Phishing Emails & Suspicious Links:** Verify sender identities and never enter credentials on unverified web links.

erqs.modelAnswer:
### Option (a): Online Store Cybersecurity Scenario

**i. Why Computer Security is Vital for an Online Business (3 Marks):**
1. **Protection of Sensitive Customer Data:** Safeguards customers' personal details, shipping addresses, and credit/debit card payment credentials from data breaches and identity theft.
2. **Prevention of Financial Loss & Business Disruption:** Prevents ransomware, fraudulent transactions, regulatory fines, and costly website downtime caused by DDoS or malware attacks.
3. **Preservation of Brand Reputation & Customer Trust:** Maintains customer confidence so shoppers feel safe purchasing from the online store without fear of compromise.

**ii. Three Specific Computer Security Measures to Protect the Online Store (3 Marks):**
1. **Strong Authentication & Access Control:** Enforce complex passwords and **Two-Factor Authentication (2FA / MFA)** for admin panels and customer accounts, along with role-based access levels.
2. **SSL/TLS Encryption & Firewalls:** Use HTTPS (`SSL/TLS`) encryption for all checkout/payment traffic and deploy a Web Application Firewall (WAF) and updated anti-malware software.
3. **Regular Software Patching & Encrypted Backups:** Keep the e-commerce platform, plugins, and server OS updated with security patches, and maintain regular off-site encrypted database backups.

### Option (b): Computer Virus and Its Transmission Vectors

**i. Description of a Computer Virus (2 Marks):**
A **computer virus** is a malicious software program that attaches itself to a legitimate host file or executable program and **replicates itself** when the infected host program is executed by a user, corrupting data, deleting files, or degrading system performance.

**ii. Four Ways by Which a Virus Can Spread in a Computer System (4 Marks):**
1. **Infected Removable Storage Media (USB Flash Drives / External Hard Drives / CDs):** Plugging in and opening files from an infected USB drive transfers the virus to the host computer.
2. **Malicious Email Attachments & Phishing Links:** Opening infected `.exe`, `.docm`, or `.zip` attachments received via email executes the embedded virus payload.
3. **Downloading Pirated or Untrusted Software from the Internet:** Installing cracked games, pirated applications, or files from unverified websites bundles hidden viruses onto the system.
4. **Local Area Networks (LAN) & Shared Network Folders:** Viruses can propagate across shared network drives when users execute infected shared files.
erqs.examinerComments: Both options were well attempted. In Part (a), candidates connected cybersecurity directly to customer data protection, financial stability, and 2FA/antivirus controls. In Part (b), candidates clearly listed USB drives, email attachments, pirated software, and internet downloads.
erqs.betterResponse: In better responses for Part (a), candidates separated the business importance points (i) from the concrete technical safeguards (ii). For Part (b), candidates defined a virus as host-dependent self-replicating malware and explained four distinct transmission vectors.
erqs.weakerResponse: In weaker responses for Part (a), candidates repeated the same point (e.g., 'install antivirus') in both parts i and ii. In Part (b), some candidates defined a virus merely as 'something that slows down the computer' without mentioning malicious code or replication.
erqs.suggestions: Practise scenario-based cybersecurity questions by distinguishing between the impact/risk of an attack (why security matters) and the technical countermeasures (encryption, 2FA, firewalls, backups, anti-malware).
